headline: Recommended to the full Council Resolution #362 supporting state legislation lifting the statewide ban on rent stabilization, after two amendments.
summary: Councilors discussed a proposed resolution on rent stabilization and heard a presentation from Homes for All Massachusetts. They approved two amendments, including removing the 5% cap on annual rent increases. They then voted 3–1 to send the amended resolution to the full Council with a positive recommendation.
decisions: Approved an amendment removing the specific 5% cap on annual rent increases and replacing it with CPI-based language, 4–0.
Approved an amendment broadening the resolution's support to legislation lifting the statewide ban on rent stabilization, 4–0.
Recommended the amended resolution to the full Council with a positive recommendation, 3–1.

City of Salem, Massachusetts 
 
“Know Your Rights Under the Open Meeting Law, M.G.L. c. 30A ss. 18-25 and  
City Ordinance Sections 2-2028 through 2-2033.” 
 
The City Council Committee on Community & Economic Development ci-posted with the Committee of the Whole __ 
will met in the Council Chamber on __July 6, 2026_____________________ at _______6:00 PM________ 
for the purpose of discussing the matters(s) listed below.  Notice of this meeting was posted on  
__________________June 29, 2026___________________ at _________9:47 A.M.__________________ 
(This meeting is being recorded) 
ATTENDANCE 
CED – Prosniewski (chair), King, Smith (left prior to public comment), Sydoriak, and Holappa. COW – Davis, Merkl, Turowski and 
Flynn. Homes for All Massachusetts – Carolyn Chou.  
ABSENT WERE:  COW – Hapworth and Varela.  
SUBJECT(S) 
#362 Rent Stabilization Resolution 
Prosniewski – King will give us some background on this proposed resolution and then we will have a presentation 
by Carolyn Chou from Homes for All Massachusetts.   
King - I urge support for rent stabilization resolution as a way to protect tenants and preserve Salem's community. 
The resolution, which was previously read in full and will be read again at the next City Council meeting if it 
advances, outlines the city's growing housing affordability crisis. Over the past five years, average rents in Salem 
have increased by nearly 35%, with more than half of renter households spending over 30% of their income on 
housing and 30% spending more than half of their income on rent. These rising costs contribute to housing 
instability and force longtime residents to leave the community. 
The resolution expresses support for pending Massachusetts legislation that would repeal the statewide ban on rent 
stabilization and allow cities and towns to decide locally whether to adopt such policies. While I personally support 
rent stabilization, the resolution is fundamentally about restoring local control.  Municipalities should have the 
authority to determine their own housing policies regardless of individual views on rent stabilization itself. 
Presentation -  
Carolyn Chou from Homes for All Massachusetts described the state's housing affordability crisis, emphasizing that 
rising rents are displacing residents in communities across Massachusetts, from the North Shore to Western 
Massachusetts and Cape Cod. She cited data showing that more than half of renters spend over one-third of their 
income on housing, while a household needs an annual income of approximately $93,000 to afford a two-bedroom 
apartment statewide with an even higher threshold in Eastern Massachusetts. Chou also highlighted the 
disproportionate impact on people of color, framing housing affordability as both an economic and racial equity 
issue.
Chou stressed that rent stabilization is not intended to be a standalone solution to the housing crisis but rather one 
of many tools needed alongside increased housing production, zoning reform, and expanded affordable housing. 
She argued that while building more housing is essential, tenants facing steep rent increases, no-fault evictions, and 
housing instability cannot wait years for new development to address the crisis. She also pointed to related 
challenges, including pressure on the state's shelter system, foreclosures, and the ongoing loss of longtime residents 
from their communities. 
Chou’s presentation outlined the coalition's legislative campaign to restore local authority over rent stabilization. 
Although a statewide ballot initiative was removed from the ballot by the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court on 
procedural grounds, Chou said it generated significant public support and awareness, collecting roughly 200,000 
signatures. The coalition is now focused on legislation that would repeal the statewide ban on rent control and allow 
municipalities to adopt local rent stabilization policies if they choose. The proposed bill would limit annual rent 
increases to the cost of living with a 5% cap, exempt owner-occupied buildings with four or fewer units and newly 
constructed housing for five years, and prohibit no-fault evictions. 
Chou also described ongoing negotiations with housing developers, real estate organizations, nonprofit housing 
providers, and state officials that resulted in a proposed compromise framework. A compromised approach would 
allow annual rent increases of inflation plus 5%, capped at 10%, extend the exemption for new construction to 15 
years, and permit larger rent increases between tenants while strengthening protections against no-fault evictions 
to discourage landlords from removing tenants solely to raise rents. Additional provisions would clarify exemptions 
for subsidized housing and procedures for landlords seeking above-cap increases for capital improvements. 
In closing, Chou emphasized that the exact details of the legislation remain open to negotiation, but argued that the 
core issue, protecting tenants from unaffordable rent increases while giving cities and towns the option to adopt 
rent stabilization, should remain a legislative priority. She stated that maintaining local authority and keeping the 
conversation active are essential steps toward addressing the state's ongoing housing affordability crisis. 
Discussion –  
The discussion clarified that S1447/H2328 serves as the current legislative vehicle for advancing rent stabilization in 
Massachusetts. While the bill reflects the original proposal, lawmakers are continuing to negotiate potential 
compromise provisions, which could be incorporated as amendments to the bill or emerge through another 
legislative vehicle as the State House process moves forward. The Senate version of the bill has recently advanced 
out of committee to the Senate Ways and Means Committee. 
Chou also highlighted recent progress, noting that Senator Joan Lovely has co-sponsored the bill, reinforcing her 
support even after the statewide ballot initiative was removed from consideration. While avoiding speaking on the 
senator's behalf, Chou said Senator Lovely, like other legislative supporters, appears open to compromise measures 
that would help advance local-option rent stabilization legislation. 
The discussion focused on clarifying details of the proposed compromise rent stabilization framework, including 
exemptions and how a future local-option system might operate. Chou explained that exemptions for owner-
occupied buildings with four or fewer units, short-term rentals, religious institutions, dormitories, and certain elder 
care facilities would remain in place because they are viewed as fundamentally different from traditional rental 
housing. They emphasized that the policy is intended to protect tenants from extreme rent increases while 
preserving flexibility for homeowners and small landlords who rely on rental income to maintain their properties. 
Councilors asked how much authority municipalities would have if the state lifted the ban on rent stabilization. The 
response suggested that cities and towns would likely adopt a standardized framework rather than creating dozens 
of entirely different systems, allowing the state to provide guidance and consistent regulations while still giving 
communities the option to opt in. Chou also explained that the compromise proposal is not yet a formal bill but
represents ongoing negotiations among tenant advocates, developers, and legislators, with the existing legislation 
serving as the primary vehicle that could still be amended as it moves through the State House. 
Several councilors raised concerns about unintended consequences, including reduced housing production, deferred 
maintenance by landlords, condo conversions, and landlords raising rents preemptively in anticipation of future 
limits. Chou argued that modern rent stabilization proposals differ significantly from older rent control systems and 
are designed to provide predictability while still allowing reasonable increases tied to inflation. She also noted that 
the legislation includes provisions intended to prevent landlords from sharply increasing rents immediately before a 
policy takes effect. 
A recurring theme throughout the discussion was local control. Multiple councilors said they were not yet certain 
whether they would ultimately support rent stabilization itself, but they believed municipalities should have the 
authority to evaluate data, consider local conditions, and decide whether such policies make sense for their 
communities. The councilors in support argued that lifting the statewide ban would allow cities like Salem to explore 
all available tools to address housing affordability without committing to any specific policy today. 
The conversation also highlighted differing interpretations of the research on rent stabilization. Some councilors 
cited studies suggesting that inflation-based rent stabilization has little long-term impact on housing production, 
while others cautioned that Salem must carefully examine potential effects on development, property owners, and 
affordability. Overall, there was broad agreement that the housing crisis is severe and that any future policy would 
need to balance tenant protections, housing production, affordability, and the realities facing both renters and 
landlords. 
Proposed Amendments –  
Councilor King proposed amendments to make the resolution more flexible and better reflect the evolving 
legislative process. The primary amendment would remove the specific language capping annual rent increases 
at 5% and replace it with language supporting a formula based on the Consumer Price Index (CPI), allowing the final 
legislation to determine the exact cap while maintaining the principle that rent increases should be tied to inflation. 
She also suggested broadening the resolution's reference to the pending legislation. Rather than specifically naming 
the current bill, she proposed revising the language to express support for Massachusetts legislation establishing 
local-option rent stabilization, recognizing that the bill could be amended or replaced as it moves through the State 
House. The goal of the amendments was to keep the resolution focused on supporting local control and rent 
stabilization generally, without tying the City Council to the exact language of a bill that is still being negotiated. 
Additional Discussion –  
The committee discussion centered on balancing the need for tenant protections with concerns about housing 
production and the evolving nature of the proposed state legislation. Councilors debated research on rent 
stabilization, with some citing studies that suggest rent regulation can reduce housing quality, discourage new 
construction, and lead to condominium conversions, while supporters argued that those findings largely reflect 
older rent control models and may not apply to modern, inflation-based rent stabilization policies. Chou emphasized 
that the proposal under consideration is intended to complement, not replace, housing production efforts and 
should be evaluated based on similar policies recently adopted in other states and municipalities. 
Several councilors expressed support for advancing the resolution because it simply asks the Legislature to restore 
local authority over rent stabilization rather than adopting a specific policy. They argued that Salem should have the 
opportunity to determine what works best for its own housing market after the Legislature completes its work. 
Supporters also stressed that rent stabilization is one tool among many needed to address the housing crisis, 
alongside zoning reform, increased housing production, transportation improvements, and anti-displacement
measures. Councilor King noted that the legislation's progress to the Senate Ways and Means Committee 
demonstrates growing momentum and argued that now is an appropriate time for Salem to signal its support for 
local control. 
Other councilors remained skeptical, questioning whether the city should endorse legislation whose final language 
has not yet been determined. They expressed concern that adopting a resolution before a final bill exists could 
weaken the value of council resolutions and argued that the city should instead wait until a specific proposal is 
available for review. Some also maintained that increasing housing supply remains the most effective long-term 
solution to affordability and cautioned that poorly designed rent stabilization policies could discourage investment 
and worsen the housing shortage. 
The discussion also addressed the role of corporate real estate investors in driving rent increases. Chou 
distinguished between large institutional investors purchasing existing multifamily properties and developers 
constructing new housing, noting that these are separate but related issues. While acknowledging the need for 
additional research, Chou cited regional studies indicating that corporate ownership has become increasingly 
common in some housing markets and contributes to higher rents and tenant displacement. 
Overall, the discussion reflected broad agreement that Salem faces a serious housing affordability crisis, but 
differing views on the best policy response. Supporters viewed the resolution as a way to preserve local decision-
making and expand the city's policy options, while opponents argued that the Council should wait for a clearly 
defined legislative proposal before formally expressing its support. 
Public Comment Summary -  
During public comment, the overwhelming majority of speakers expressed support for the resolution, arguing that 
Salem should urge the state to restore local authority over rent stabilization. Many emphasized that the resolution 
does not implement rent stabilization itself but simply gives municipalities the ability to decide whether to adopt 
such policies. Speakers repeatedly described the housing crisis as an urgent issue that requires multiple solutions, 
with rent stabilization serving as one tool alongside increased housing production, zoning reform, and other 
affordability measures. 
Several residents shared personal experiences with housing insecurity and rising rents. Speakers recounted being 
forced to move repeatedly because of annual rent increases, struggling to afford basic necessities while paying rent, 
watching family members and friends leave Massachusetts due to housing costs, and witnessing longtime Salem 
residents displaced after buildings changed ownership. Others described growing up in overcrowded housing or 
experiencing homelessness, arguing that housing stability is essential for preserving Salem's diverse, working-class 
community. 
Supporters also challenged arguments that rent stabilization would significantly reduce housing production or 
discourage property maintenance. Some cited academic research suggesting that modern rent stabilization policies 
tied to inflation have little long-term effect on new construction, while distinguishing them from older rent control 
systems. Others argued that the housing market has changed dramatically since the COVID-19 pandemic and that 
rising rents are increasingly driven by speculative investment and market pressures rather than operating costs 
alone. 
While broadly supportive of the resolution's goal, a few speakers urged the Council to amend or broaden the 
language. They expressed concern that the resolution specifically references the current legislative bill, which they 
viewed as more restrictive than the compromise language currently under discussion. These speakers encouraged 
the Council to instead endorse local control over rent stabilization more generally while also advocating for 
complementary housing policies, including zoning reform, parking reform, higher-density housing, streamlined 
permitting, and other state legislation designed to increase housing production.
Overall, public comment reflected broad agreement that Salem faces a serious housing affordability crisis and that 
local communities should have greater authority to respond. Supporters urged the Council to pass the resolution as 
a statement to the Legislature that cities and towns deserve the option to consider rent stabilization, while others 
encouraged refining the resolution to better balance tenant protections with continued housing production and 
long-term affordability. 
Note: Smith left due to a family matter. 
The committee approved two amendments before voting to advance the resolution. The first amendment removed 
the specific 5% cap on annual rent increases and replaced it with broader language supporting rent increases based 
on a formula tied to the Consumer Price Index (CPI), making the resolution flexible enough to accommodate 
changes to the legislation as it moves through the State House. Motion by King and seconded.  Motion carries 4–0. 
The committee then approved a second amendment to broaden the resolution's support for state legislation. Rather 
than referencing a specific bill by title, the amended language expresses support for legislation lifting the statewide 
ban on rent stabilization, reflecting that the final legislative vehicle or language may change during the legislative 
process. This is the last sentence on the first page of the resolution.  They also remove the “the” before legislation in 
the same sentence.  Motion by King and seconded.   Motion carries 4–0. 
Following the amendments, King moved to recommend the amended resolution to the full Council with a positive 
recommendation. During discussion, supporters said the amendments strengthened the resolution by focusing on 
the principle of local control rather than a specific bill whose language is still evolving. Councilor King thanked fellow 
councilors for a productive committee discussion, noting that the collaborative process had improved the 
resolution. 
The committee then voted to send the amended resolution to the full Council with a positive recommendation, 
where it will be considered at the next council meeting. Motion carries 3–1. 
On the motion of C. King, the meeting adjourned at 8:01 P.M. 
 
       Conrad Prosniewski                       MBC 
         (Chairperson)
